items.prompt: How does this unit define a "feature"?
choices: A fact about the product: what it contains, how it works, its specifications — true regardless of who's listening
The price a customer pays for a product
An outcome the listener personally experiences
A marketing slogan used to sell a product
items.reference:
🧪 Feature — a fact about the product, true for everyone
💰 Value — what that fact means for THIS listener
items.explanation: A feature is a factual property of the product — what it contains, how it works, its specifications — and it's true no matter who's listening, unlike value which depends on the specific listener.

items.prompt: Which of these is an example of a feature, per this unit's definition?
choices: "You'll save about $1,028 in year one"
"It has an activated carbon filter"
"Your water will taste like bottled water"
"You won't need to buy bottled water anymore"
items.reference:
🧪 Feature — a fact about the product, true for everyone
💰 Value — what that fact means for THIS listener
items.explanation: "It has an activated carbon filter" is a factual property of the product itself — true regardless of who's listening — which is exactly what makes it a feature rather than a value statement.

items.prompt: How does this unit define "value"?
choices: The list price of the product
What a feature means for a specific listener — the outcome they get, in terms they already care about
The total number of features a product has
How much the product weighs
items.reference:
🧪 Feature — a fact about the product, true for everyone
💰 Value — what that fact means for THIS listener
items.explanation: Value is what a feature *means* for a specific listener — expressed as an outcome they get, in terms they already care about, like time saved, money saved, or a problem going away.

items.prompt: In the water filter scenario, what was the value statement, as opposed to the feature statement?
choices: "Activated carbon filter, 10-cup capacity, BPA-free plastic"
"Tap water that tastes like bottled water, for about $1,028 less in year one"
Both statements are equally feature statements
Neither statement describes value at all
items.reference:
🧪 Feature — a fact about the product, true for everyone
💰 Value — what that fact means for THIS listener
items.explanation: The value statement — taste like bottled water and a specific dollar savings figure — expresses the outcome in terms (taste, money) the listener already cares about, without requiring background about filtration technology.

items.prompt: What is the "translation gap", as this unit defines it?
choices: The time it takes to translate a pitch into another language
The mental work a listener has to do to get from a feature to why it matters to them
The difference in price between two competing products
The gap between a product's release date and its marketing launch
items.reference:
🌉 Translation gap — work needed to get from feature to "why it matters"
🛑 A wide gap means most listeners give up before crossing it
items.explanation: The translation gap is the mental work a listener has to do to connect a feature to a reason it matters to them — a wide gap means most listeners simply give up before making that connection themselves.

items.prompt: What happens when a pitch leaves a wide translation gap unaddressed?
choices: Listeners always successfully cross it on their own
Most listeners give up before crossing it, since feature framing assumes they'll do the translation work themselves
The gap automatically closes itself over time
It has no effect on whether the listener understands the pitch
items.reference:
🌉 Translation gap — work needed to get from feature to "why it matters"
🛑 A wide gap means most listeners give up before crossing it
items.explanation: A wide, unaddressed translation gap means most listeners give up before crossing it — feature framing assumes the listener will do the connecting work unprompted, which most people won't do, especially without relevant background.

items.prompt: What does this unit mean by "audience-relevant terms"?
choices: Technical jargon specific to the product's internal vocabulary
Units of meaning a listener already understands and cares about, like money, time, comfort, or risk
The exact words used in the product's instruction manual
Terms only used by industry experts
items.reference:
💵 Audience-relevant: money, time, comfort, risk, effort
🔬 Not audience-relevant: filter types, technical specs, jargon
items.explanation: Audience-relevant terms are units of meaning the listener already understands and cares about — money, time, comfort, risk, effort — as opposed to terms specific to the product's own internal, technical vocabulary.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT an audience-relevant term, per this unit?
choices: Money saved per year
Time saved per day
"Activated carbon filtration technology"
A problem that goes away
items.reference:
💵 Audience-relevant: money, time, comfort, risk, effort
🔬 Not audience-relevant: filter types, technical specs, jargon
items.explanation: "Activated carbon filtration technology" is product-specific technical vocabulary — the listener still has to translate it into something they care about, unlike money, time, or a resolved problem, which are already meaningful without extra background.

"Activated carbon filter, 10-cup capacity, BPA-free plastic"
"The best pitcher on the market today"
"A pitcher that filters water instantly"

💰 Pitch B: value (taste, $1,028.50 first-year savings)

choices: Glazed eyes for both pitches equally

Immediate purchase after hearing either pitch

items.explanation: The scenario describes glazed eyes in response to the feature-only pitch, but genuine interest ("wait, how much?") in response to the value-first pitch — the same product, described two different ways.

items.prompt: According to the opening scenario, what did both pitches have in common?
choices: They described two completely different products
They described the exact same water filter pitcher — only the framing differed
Neither pitch contained any true information
Both pitches used identical wording

items.explanation: Both pitches described the exact same underlying product — nothing about the pitcher itself changed between the two versions, only which facts got stated and how they were framed.

items.prompt: Per the unit's own answer to its opening question, why did only the value pitch make the listener want to buy the product?
choices: Because the value pitch was louder
Because it described what the product does for the listener — a concrete, felt difference expressed in terms they didn't need special knowledge to understand
Because the value pitch was shorter than the feature pitch
Because the feature pitch contained false information
items.reference:
🧪 Feature pitch: describes what the product IS
💰 Value pitch: describes what it DOES for the listener
items.explanation: The unit's answer is that the value pitch described a concrete, felt outcome in the listener's own terms — no special knowledge required — while the feature pitch merely described what the product is, leaving the listener to do the connecting work themselves.

items.prompt: What does the unit say feature framing assumes about the listener?
choices: That the listener already has all the information they need to buy the product
That the listener will do the translation work themselves, figuring out unprompted why the feature matters to their life
That the listener doesn't need any information at all
That the listener will automatically distrust the pitch
items.reference:
🧪 Feature pitch: describes what the product IS
💰 Value pitch: describes what it DOES for the listener
items.explanation: Feature framing assumes the listener will independently figure out why a given fact matters to their own life — most listeners won't do that unprompted, especially without the background to make the connection easily.

items.prompt: L2 notes that every rung of the "so what" ladder is still true. What does this imply about climbing the ladder?
choices: Climbing the ladder requires inventing new facts not already present

Why: Each rung is still true — what changes is which fact gets stated out loud.
items.explanation: L2 emphasizes that climbing the ladder doesn't invent anything — every rung is derived from the same underlying true facts; what changes is simply which of those true facts actually gets spoken aloud to the listener.

items.prompt: What is the "curse of knowledge", as described in L2?
choices: A bias where knowing something makes it hard to imagine not knowing it, causing you to underestimate how much translation someone else needs
A legal restriction on sharing certain kinds of product information
The tendency for experts to always give the worst pitches on purpose
A term for products that are too complicated to ever explain simply
items.reference:
🧠 Curse of knowledge — hard to imagine not knowing what you know
📉 Leads to underestimating how much translation others need
items.explanation: The curse of knowledge is a bias where, once you know something well, it becomes hard to imagine not knowing it — which causes you to underestimate how much translation work someone without your background actually needs.

items.prompt: Per L2, why does someone who knows a product well tend to stop at step 1 of the "so what" ladder?
choices: Because step 1 facts are the ones they know best, and those facts no longer feel like they need explaining to them personally
Because they're deliberately trying to confuse the listener
Because step 1 is always the most persuasive statement possible
Because later steps on the ladder are usually false
items.reference:
🧠 Curse of knowledge — hard to imagine not knowing what you know
📉 Leads to underestimating how much translation others need
items.explanation: L2 explains that the person describing a product tends to know the step-1 facts best, and because those facts feel self-evident to them personally, they underestimate how much translation a listener without that background actually needs.

items.prompt: What does L2 say is the fix for the curse of knowledge, as it applies to pitching a product?
choices: Knowing less about the product
Deliberately climbing the ladder every time, rather than trusting the listener will climb it on their own
Never mentioning any features at all, under any circumstances
Hiring someone else to give every pitch instead
items.reference:
🧠 Curse of knowledge — hard to imagine not knowing what you know
📉 Leads to underestimating how much translation others need
items.explanation: L2's fix isn't to know less — it's to deliberately climb the "so what" ladder every time rather than trusting the listener will do it unprompted, since the curse of knowledge means that trust is usually misplaced.
